questions.title_en: Was Shlomo Molcho HY”D the author of Shalom Aleichem?
questions.question:
I recently watched a video claiming that Shlomo Molcho hy”d was the author of the piyut Shalom Aleichem. Does anyone have any sources for this, or does anyone know of anyone else to whom it is attributed?

(The source of Shalom Aleichem has already been discussed here, but I haven’t seen this particular legend addressed.)

answers.text:
The Book: "Sefer: Minhag Tov" which seems to have been written in the year (about) 1273-1275;(maybe as late as 1300?), has a list of Jewish customs. One of them (#36), states:

"And it is a good custom on Friday nights, when we come (home) from the Synagogue, to go right away next to the candles lit for the honor of the Sabbath, which we made the blessing upon, and stand next to both of them and say: "Oh angels of mercy and peace, May your coming be for peace, May your coming be for peace, Upon you should be peace, For all of you there should be peace..." And so too have I found written that Rabbi Aharon of Regensburg acustomed himself to do so."

"Sefaria.org" writes the following information about this Book, showing the author is assumed to be an Italian Rabbi of the middle ages:

"Sefer Minhag Tov, an anonymous treatise composed circa 1275, whose author may have studied with northern French Tosafists but who certainly did study with R. Moses ben Meir of Ferrera and perhaps settled in Bari or Taranto..." From Kabbalah: Journal for the Study of Jewish Mystical Texts, Volume 6 pg. 144 (Courtesy of R. Joel Zeff)."

It therefore seems that the original words of at least a proto-Shalom Aleychem liturgy was already in use as early as the mid thirteenth or even twelfth century and probably has roots beforehand as well.

Therefore it would seem to be an error to attribute the creation of the liturgy to Solomon Molcho, or any Jewish figure who lived and was active in the early 1500's.

Here is the link to Sefer Minhag Tov:

https://hebrewbooks.org/pdfpager.aspx?req=8903&st=&pgnum=12&hilite=

questions.title_he: Can one fulfill the obligation of eating a כזית of פת on the first night of Sukkos with cake?
questions.question:
There is an obligation to eat a כזית of פת on the first night of Sukkos. (Orach Chaim 639:3)

Can one fulfill that obligation with something that is Mezonos, such as cake?

answers.text:
SA 639:3

אכילה בסוכה בליל יום טוב הראשון חובה אפי' אכל כזית פת יצא

Eating in the Sukkah on the first night, is obligatory. If he ate an olive sized amount of bread, he has fulfilled his obligation.

The Biur Hagra 639:1 understand that the yerushalmi (sukka 2:7) asked if one can be יוצא with מיני תרגימה and the yerushalmi concludes that not. The Gra understand that that is the reason for the SA to explicitly writeפת

ס"ג אפי' אכל כו'. ירושלמי שם והביאו תוס' והרא"ש אי מה להלן עד שיאכל כזית דגן כו'. ומיבעיא ליה אי יוצא במיני תרגימא וז"ש כזית פת לחומרא:

The MB 639:21 rules as much.

כא) פת - ולא מיני תרגימא דספיקא דאורייתא הוא וגם לא פת כיסנין אלא פת גמור [שע"ת]:

In conclusionOne must eat bread on the first night in order to be יוצא the Mitzva of Sukka on the first night

questions.title_he: Is there ever a time when one would need to repeat מעין שלש in order to mention Shabbat or Yom Tov?
questions.question: If one does not have bread to eat on Shabbat, but he has Mezonot - not enough to be Kovei’a Seudah - would he need to repeat Al Hamichya if he forgot to mention Shabbat?

answers.text:
No, there is no need to repeat Me’ein Shalosh if one forgot to mention Shabbos or Yom Tov.

Mishnah Berurah 208:58:

מעין המאורע - היינו קודם שאומר כי אתה ה' טוב ומטיב יאמר בשבת ורצה והחליצנו ביום השבת הזה וביום טוב אומר וזכרנו לטובה ביום חג פלוני הזה וכן בר"ח יאמר וזכרנו לטובה ביום ר"ח הזה ובדיעבד אפילו לא הזכיר מעין המאורע יצא:

questions.title_he: Why do so many chazzanim skip "אמרינו האזינה ה' בינה הגיגנו" in שמע קולנו?
questions.question:
Approximately half of the (Ashk'nazi) chazzanim I've heard leading s'lichot either skip or say silently "אמרינו האזינה ה' בינה הגיגנו" in שמע קולנו.

I haven't seen any siddurim say to do this, so I've asked several of those chazzanim why they do it, and the response has always been that they've heard others do that.

I'm therefore curious what the source is for this practice.

I'm aware that the following phrase, יהיו לרצון, is supposed to be said silently.

בסדר אזי אין קשר ,אז אוסיף בשאלה במסעת חולין כ ו כז .
שכן ברש"י אין שחיטה לעוף מהתורה

משמע אין השחיטה של העוף מן התורה,אולם נפסק כדי להפריד,אך אין זו יכולה להיות סיבה להפריד 

ב"ה שלום וברכה 
ההבדל הוא שבעוף מספיק סימן אחד ובבהמה צריך שנים.

questions.title_en: L'chatchila Ariber: what does it mean and where does it come from?
questions.question:
There seems to be a famous saying from the Rebbe Maharash, Rabbi Shmuel Schneersohn (1834 - 1882):

די וועלט זאגט, אז מ'קען ניט ארונטער דארף מען אריבער, און איך האלט אז מ'דארף לכתחילה אריבער

The world says that if you can’t go underneath, you must go over. But I say that you should go over to begin with.

The Lubavitcher Rebbe often quotes this, for example in Igros Kodesh (here).

What does "L'chatchila Ariber" means, where does it come from, and what is the lesson we are meant to take from it according to the (Chabad) Rebbeim?

answers.text:
As a starting point see here:

This idea of leaping over obstacles from the very beginning became a symbol of what the Rebbe called a Baal Shem’ske behavior, akin to the conduct of the Baal Shem Tov. It means rising above challenges, never letting obstacles deter you from your path.

There’s a famous story about the Besht, who instructed his students to collect icicles from the roof and then lit them like candles. This was a play on words in Yiddish, in which icicles are called אייז ליכטעלעך = Ice candles. He did this to illustrate the concept of leaping over. The world may say that icicles cannot burn like candles, but the Besht showed that with faith, even seemingly impossible things can be achieved.

In life, people often say we must work within the confines of the world, to be realistic and avoid risks. But the Rebbe teaches us to rise above, to take risks, because we are not limited by the constraints of the world. This attitude leads to success beyond limitations.

The Rebbe loved this idea and encouraged his followers to embrace it.

questions.title_he: אמירת וארשתיך בהנחת תפילין דרבנו תם
questions.question:
למרות שלא מברכים על הנחת תפילין דרבנו תם, האם יש לומר שלושת הפסוקים של וארשתיך בכריכת הרצועה על אצבע? תודה!

שלום וברכה
אכן, יש מעלה לומר פסוקים אלו גם בהנחת תפילין דרבינו תם.

Famously in this week's parshah וְזֹ֣את הַבְּרָכָ֗ה V'zot haBrakah Moses our master gives his last will and testament, his ברכה berakah, benediction to each of the 12 Tribes of Israel

But as many readers have pointed out, and commentators have addressed: not all 12 of the tribes appear to be listed.

The Tribe of Simeon, שמעון Shimon, appears to be missing.

Elsewhere commentators have wrestled with this issue, variously. Rashi says that:

לְשִׁמְעוֹן מִתּוֹךְ בִּרְכוֹתָיו שֶׁל יְהוּדָה

"Shimon's blessing is within Yehudah's"

שְׁמַ֤ע יְהֹוָה֙ ק֣וֹל יְהוּדָ֔ה וְאֶל־עַמּ֖וֹ תְּבִיאֶ֑נּוּ יָדָיו֙ רָ֣ב ל֔וֹ וְעֵ֥זֶר מִצָּרָ֖יו תִּהְיֶֽה׃

Shema'Ya (שמע יהוה), the voice of Judah: restore him to his people, through his own hands strive for him. Help him against his foes.

Remarkably Rashi says that Shema'Ya (שמע יהוה) is Shimon's name! Tying back to the story of his birth to our foremother Leah:

וַתַּ֣הַר עוֹד֮ וַתֵּ֣לֶד בֵּן֒ וַתֹּ֗אמֶר כִּֽי־שָׁמַ֤ע יְהֹוָה֙ כִּֽי־שְׂנוּאָ֣ה אָנֹ֔כִי וַיִּתֶּן־לִ֖י גַּם־אֶת־זֶ֑ה וַתִּקְרָ֥א שְׁמ֖וֹ שִׁמְעֽוֹן׃

And she conceived again and bore a son, and declared, “This is because יהוה heard that I was unloved so he has given me this one also”; so she named him Shimon: G!d heard.

Besides the obvious connection between the names Yishma'EL-Shema'Ya-Shimon (God will hear, G!d hears, G!d has heard) and the interesteing coincidence that Yishma'El also has 12 tribes .... the biographers have tried to establish this connection between Shimon & Yishma'El

Indeed as the Jewish Encylopedia records: "Many attempts have been made to connect Simeon with Ishmael and Massa, and with the founders of Mecca" 1 but it cites no source.

So: is there more to this story and is Yishma'El Shimon and is Shimon Yishma'El?

questions.question:
So far as I know the earliest explicit mention of these is in the tanaic/amoraic literature.

answers.text:

questions.title_en: What would be the punishment for a pedophilic act/statutory rape according to halacha?
questions.question: Would it necessitate capital punishment, public humiliation like flogging, or something less severe? Sources please.

answers.text:
There is no standalone commandment against non penetrative pedophilia but it could be a damage.

Bava Kamma lists the categories of damage that could occur.

Nézek: Damage or tort Tsa'ár: Pain or suffering Shavát: Stoppage of work Ripui: Cost of cure Bṓšeṯ: Shame or disgrace

If there was no physical or mental injury and all parties lived in a paedo society where to be molested wasn't considered disgraceful, there would be no damages.

However, the Rabbis (or the King) have a secular authority to flog, execute people, and impose fines even when there aren't kosher witnesses or the act isn't a formal sin.

But is any particular action necessitated? There is a commandment not to stand idly when your neighbor's blood is being spilled so it would make sense that executing, imprisoning, banishing etc. the pedophile would be an obligation and I'm sure some rabbis will rule that way, but I don't think it's explicitly codified in the Mishna Brura or Shulchan Aruch.

see below regarding this authority: https://jcpa.org/article/horaat-shaah-the-emergency-principle-in-jewish-law-and-a-contemporary-application/

questions.title_en: Connection Between V'zos Habracha & Bereishes
questions.question: On Simchas Torah we read the end of V'zos Habracha and the begining of Bereishes - is there any special connection between them? Maybe something similiar about the Pesukim or the story line?

answers.text:
Rashi on the word בראשית says:

בשביל התורה שנקראת ראשית… ובשביל ישראל שנקראו ראשית.

Simply put, the world was created for the two things called Reishis: the Torah and Bnei Yisrael.

The blessings of Bnei Yisrael are thus very much intertwined with both the creation of the world and the beginning of the Torah.

A year ago, I wrote this pertinent article, where just past the halfway point is a section beginning with the caption Comparing Bereishis to V'zos - המגיד מראשית אחרית and then has the subsequent section beginning Let's Explore How וזאת הברכה is Very Connected to בראשית!. There you will find some interesting connections between the very end of the Torah and the very beginning.

Among those connections is a great one that I can briefly highlight here. It's based on Rav Chaim Kanievsky's take on the Rokeach's take on the following well known Rashi:

בראשית ברא - אֵין הַמִּקְרָא הַזֶּה אוֹמֵר אֶלָּא דָּרְשֵׁנִי, כְּמוֹ שֶׁדְּרָשׁוּהוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ

בִּשְׁבִיל הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁנִקְרֵאת "רֵאשִׁית דַּרְכּוֹ" (משלי ח:כב)

וּבִשְׁבִיל יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁנִקְרְאוּ "רֵאשִׁית תְּבוּאָתֹה" (ירמיה ב:ג)

The peirush of the רוקח on the end of וזאת הברכה appears below:
(יצא לאור ע"י יואל קלוגמאן תשל"ט - תשמ"א, הערות מאת הרה"ג ר' חיים קניבסקי)

While the dashes indicate that parts of the original manuscript of the רוקח were unclear, Rav Chaim Kanievsky's notes indicate the following educated guess to the lines:

החומש מתחיל בראשית ומסיים ישראל ואין ראשית אלא ישראל (ירמיהו ב) "קודש ישראל ראשית", בראשית בגימטריא ישראל בחר בעמים. לכך סיים התורה ישראל, התורה כלולה בישראל

that the Chumash begins with the word בראשית and ends with the word ישראל since ישראל itself is considered a type of ראשית and therefore the Torah is filled with ישראל from beginning to end.

questions.title_en: Why did Hashem create the Livyasan?
questions.question:
In Parshas Bereishis it says that Hashem created the large fish. Rashi explains that it is referring to the two Livyasans (Leviathans) that Hashem created - a male & a female. He then says that Hashem had to kill the female, because if they would be able to reproduce, there would be no more room in the world for anything else since they are so big.

It is a known thing that Hashem took the Livyasan out of this world and is saving it for a big feast for the Tzadikim in Olam Haba when Moshiach comes - so why did Hashem create the Livyasan if He knew that He wasn't going to need it until Moshiach comes, years later?

questions.title_en: Why did Hashem create the Ohr HaGanuz?
questions.question: Rashi says on a Pasuk in Parshas Bereishes that Hashem created the Ohr HaGanuz / a very special light. Hashem then took away this light and reserved it for when Moshiach comes - so if Hashem knew that he wasn't going to need this light until later on, then why did he create it?

answers.text:
If He created on six days, rested on the seventh, and thousands of years later worked an eighth day we wouldn't have our convenient weekly cycle.

Seven is also an important numerology number and if God was known to make extra creations now and then, it would break the significance of the 7 days of creation and the other 7s we have.

I have 3 answers to this question:

  1. There is a Pasuk in Koheles that reads:

מַה־שֶּֽׁהָיָה֙ ה֣וּא שֶׁיִּֽהְיֶ֔ה וּמַ֨ה־שֶּׁנַּֽעֲשָׂ֔ה ה֖וּא שֶׁיֵּֽעָשֶׂ֑ה וְאֵ֥ין כָּל־חָדָ֖שׁ תַּ֥חַת הַשָּֽׁמֶשׁ

"What has been is what will be, and what has been done is what will be done, and there is nothing new under the sun"*

This shows that there is nothing new ever created and that everything was create originally by the creation of the world.

  1. So that people can find the Ohr HaGanuz through learning Torah.
  2. The Zohar says that once a week on Shabbos this light is shown on us, and therefore Hashem created it by Brias HaOlam.

questions.title_en: Grammar of Pausal Forms in Selichos, Hoshanos, etc
questions.question:
In the S'lichos of Nusach Lita we read towards the end a tefila, which is stated using the ךָ-ֶ (-ekha) pausal form:

עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן אֲמִתֶּךָ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן בְּרִיתֶךָ. עֲשֵׁה לְמַֽעַן גָּדְלֶךָ וְתִפְאַרְתֶּךָ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן דָּתֶךָ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן הוֹדֶךָ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן וִעוּדֶךָ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן זִכְרֶךָ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן חַסְדֶּךָ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַעַן טוּבֶךָ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן יִחוּדֶךָ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן כְּבוֹדֶךָ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן לִמּוּדֶךָ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן מַלְכוּתֶךָ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן נִצְחֶךָ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן סוֹדֶךָ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן עֻזֶּךָ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן פְּאֵרֶךָ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן צִדְקָתֶךָ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן קְדֻשָּׁתֶךָ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן רַחֲמֶֽיךָ הָרַבִּים. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן שְׁכִינָתֶךָ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן תְּהִלָּתֶךָ.

In the Yom Kippur Nussach Ashkenaz, the same tefilah is stated in the ךְ-ָ (-akh) pausal form:

עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן אֲמִתָּךְ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן בְּרִיתָךְ. עֲשֵׁה לְמַֽעַן גָּדְלָךְ וְתִפְאַרְתָּךְ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן דָּתָךְ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן הוֹדָךְ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן וִעוּדָךְ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן זִכְרָךְ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן חַסְדָּךְ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַעַן טוּבָךְ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן יִחוּדָךְ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן כְּבוֹדָךְ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן לִמּוּדָךְ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן מַלְכוּתָךְ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן נִצְחָךְ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן סוֹדָךְ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן עֻזָּךְ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן פְּאֵרָךְ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן צִדְקָתָךְ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן קְדֻשָּׁתָךְ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן רַחֲמֶֽיךָ הָרַבִּים. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן שְׁכִינָתָךְ. עֲשֵׂה לְמַֽעַן תְּהִלָּתָךְ.

By comparison, on Succos we say all the Hoshanos in the later form. What is the origin of these differences and what is the correct way to say?

I also saw a similar difference between some siddurim in pointing the piyut Y'did Nefesh (Seuda Shlishi of Shabbos). What is interesting, is that everybody sings the melody as if it was written for the -akh form but incorrectly pronounces the nekudos of the printed -ekha form, especially the first line. The same problem is with the last stanza of Dror Yikra (thanks Double AA).

questions.title_en: Why Would a Kohen Create Pigul? Weaponization?
questions.question:
One who eats Pigul is Chayav Karet (see Zevachim, Mishna 2:2). There are several ways to create Pigul, but a simple case is such: Priest A is receiving the blood of a sacrificial animal, and he thinks about eating the meat of the same animal beyond its allotted time. One must discontinue the sacrificial service. But if the service is continued and certain conditions come true and the blood is sprinkled ... anyone who eats the meat of that sacrifice, even within the permitted time, receives Karet. Kohanim, however, are presumably scrupulous in their activities. Why would a Kohen do this?

In fact, the Mishna in Gitin 5:4 states:

הַכֹּהֲנִים שֶׁפִּגְּלוּ בַמִּקְדָּשׁ מְזִידִין, חַיָּבִין.Kohanim who intentionally create Pigul in the Temple are liable (for monetary damages to the owner of the sacrifice).

The Yachin/Tiferet Yisrael states:

מזידין שידע שמזיקו בזה:

Intentionally (means) that he knew he would harm/ruin (the property of another via) this (act)

The Yachin goes on to say:

ונ״ל דלהכי לא נקיט ה״נ שוגגין פטורים, מדאינו מצוי שלא ידע הכהן שמפסיד הקרבן כשיפגלו ויהיה שוגג, דהרי למד דיני קרבן ה׳ שנים קודם שנכנס לעבודה. It appears to me that the reason that (the Mishna) did not similarly state (if Kohanim created Pigul)"by accident they are not liable", is because it is not common for a Kohen not to know that he ruins the sacrifice/property when he does Pigul (the case of accident does not normatively exist) for a Kohen studies the laws of sacrifices five years before initiating his service.

Thus, it is clear that accidental Pigul is a misnomer and not part of the discussion; Kohanim knew about the ramifications and consequences of their sacrificial actions. What is the motive? A Kohen weaponizing a sacrifice - intentionally, on occasion, to thwart the penitence of another?

The weaponization theory is not that far-fetched:

בן ידיד הלכות גניבה פרק ב הלכה א כהנים שפגלו במקדש לחבירו הוא שהזיק כדי שיביא אחר או שלא יעשה רצונו שלא הביא דורון. Ben Ydid Laws of Theft, 2:1 - Kohanim who create Pigul in the Temple, he has harmed his friend in order to (force him) to bring another (sacrifice) or so that (God) not do his (friend's) will because he did not bring a gift.

answers.text:
It is difficult, if not impossible, to infer any motive from the actual Kohanim from that time. And I couldn't think of a description somewhere where Pigul has actually occurred, and than explained why it had occurred. We are left to infer.

The Mishnah presents a scenario where a priest, who is ideally highly scrupulous, introduces an improper intent that could invalidate an entire sacrifice. Because Pigul requires intent we can rule out that the laws of Pigul is used to cover for any mistakes, or 'young trainee'-situations. Zevachim doesn’t elaborate much on why a Kohen might intentionally think improper thoughts during the sacrificial service, leaving us to wonder whether it was:

  • A rare but real occurrence that needed a legal framework,
  • More of a theoretical construct to safeguard the sanctity of the Temple rituals, or
  • Addressing concerns about potential spiritual negligence or internal conflicts among even our most dedicated people.

As mentioned in the comments by @Double_AA, even a momentary lapse in judgement for whatever personal reasons could create a situation of pigul; and the Mishna seems to (pre-emptively?) provide a legal framework for handling this for whenever it would occur.

Without any known anecdotes we are left to imagine scenarios where even a Kohen Gadol would suffer a momentary lapse in judgement or succumb to a spiritual struggle, or chas weshalom act out of malicious intent.

questions.title_en: Is it permissible to speak while shaking the lulav and etrog in the sukkah?
questions.question: After saying the bracha, is it permissible to speak while shaking the lulav and etrog in the sukkah?

answers.text:
There would be an issue of talking between the bracha for making a mitzva and performing the mitzva. For example, when you make a beracha to put on the tallis, you shouldn't speak u til you actually wore the tallis .

In the case of the lulav, you shouldn't speak between the beracha and the נטילה. But keep in mind that the moment you hold all 4 species in the right direction (estrogen with the pittum side up) you were technically already yotze the mitzva. So talking thereafter, even while you are performing the minhag of shaking the lulav in all directions, isn't a problem, because it is not a hefsek between the berach and the mitzvah performance.

See SA SA OC 651:5, that one needs to make the beracha before holding the etrog the correct way, so that the beracha is made prior to being יוצא the mitzva. This proves that just holding the species the correct way is enough to be יוצא.

questions.question:

Sifrei Torah today are written in kethav Ashurith, the Aramaic square script:

questions.title_en: Who are the lulav and the hadasim?
questions.question:
There is a popular midrash that the four species on Sukkos represent four kinds of people. I usually see it in the form where the smell corresponds to mitzvos and the taste corresponds to Torah learning (example):

  • Esrog: Torah and mitzvos
  • Lulav: Torah but not mitzvos
  • Hadasim: Mitzvos but not Torah
  • Aravos: No Torah and no mitzvos

This is the version of the midrash in Vayikra Rabbah and Pesikta Derav Kahana.

R' Elazar Hakalir's siluk for the first day of Sukkos says the opposite: taste is mitzvos and smell is Torah, with the result that the lulav and hadasim are switched with respect to the common version.

Dr. Goldschmidt in the footnotes cites both midrashim, but (uncharacteristically) doesn't point out the switch. Are there any other old or recent sources that have the switched version? Does anyone mention the difference or discuss the implications of taste and smell corresponding to one or the other?

I would have thought that back in Europe when people were still saying piyutim, they'd have been more familiar with the Kalir's version, so it's interesting that the other one became more popular.

questions.title_en: Is there a Mitzvah to increase in the size of the Matzah and Maror?
questions.question:
The Shulchan Aruch (Orach Chaim 656:1) says that there is a Mitzvah to increase in the size of the Esrog more than the required Shiur, and the Magen Avraham there holds that this applies to all Mitzvah-articles as well, such as a Shofar and a Sefer Torah.

questions.title_en: Can an Orthodox Jew attend a Christmas party?
questions.question: Can an Orthodox Jew attend a Christmas party? Many Jewish people have Christian friends, and those that have undergone a conversion to Judaism typically also have Christian friends (as well relationships with the family that they grew up with). Is there anything that would make this forbidden?

answers.text:
The main issue may possibly be the Gemara (Avodah Zarah 8a) that states that "Jews in the Diaspora worship idolatry in purity". What does this mean? When a Gentile makes a personal celebration (like a wedding for their child), he invites Jews to the party and they attend. Even though they eat their own kosher food, the Torah considers it as if they are eating idolatrous sacrifices from the host. It says, “Lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land, and they prostitute themselves to their gods and sacrifice to their gods, and one of them invites you and you eat of his sacrifice” (Ex. 34:15). The end of the verse implies that you may not accept an invitation from an idolater and, if you do, it is as if you are eating from his idolatrous sacrifice.

This being said- it is quite possible that these aren’t really "religious" celebrations. Most large companies nowadays try to accommodate people of all religions and do not have explicitly religious celebrations. These “holiday” parties and are entirely secular. If something even remotely religious happens, like singing Christmas carols or someone entering dressed as Santa Claus, I would possibly leave (Although I’m not convinced that either of the two examples I mentioned are actually religious). But really we are just talking about a neutral holiday party.

Gentiles today do not worship idolatry and, even if they do, they do not thank their god that a Jew who works in their legal department attended a mandatory business party.

People may get very offended if Jews as a group, or even religious Jews as a group, refuse to go to the company’s holiday party. The company spends a lot of money on what they consider to be a morale booster and if you refuse to participate, especially after they make certain that there is nothing religiously offensive and glatt kosher food is available, you are undermining company morale and offending executives.

sources for more details:

Shulchan Arukh (Yoreh De’ah 152:1)- see discussions of shach and Taz of biblical or rabbinic.

Rav Menasheh Klein (Mishneh Halakhos 7:118) rules like Taz (not allowed)

Levush explicitly rules that eivah (offending) overrides the prohibition against attending a Gentile party (to which the Taz objects)

Rav Moshe Feinstein (Iggeros Moshe, Yoreh De’ah 2:117) seems to rule like Shach, allowing it in cases of eivah.

R. Ari Wasserman has a section in his book Making it work dedicated to the question of attending non-Jewish social gatherings and holiday parties.

He identifies several issues:

  • A Torah prohibition of eating at a non-Jewish wedding (see YD 152:1)
  • Concerns of idolatry
  • Concerns that it would lead to intermarriage
  • Having to balance the above concerns with the need to maintain cordial relations with non-Jews (eivah)

Regarding office parties specifically, he brings multiple opinions, from those strictly forbidding them (e.g., when no legitimate need, parties before non-Jewish holidays with food and alcohol served, or mixed dancing) to certain opinions permitting them (e.g., where non-attendance might bring significant repercussions and parties are professional rather than for enjoyment).

R. Doniel Neustadt (here) brings the following:

It depends on the type of party the company is having. Many times, a company’s holiday party has nothing to do with the celebration of the holiday; rather it is an employee appreciation party that happens to take place during the holiday season. There is no halachic objection to attending such a party. But if the intention of the party is to celebrate the actual non-Jewish holiday, it would be forbidden for a Jew to attend.

However, even if the party is not intended to celebrate a non-Jewish holiday, non-Jewish office parties are hardly the place for an observant Jew to be. The mode of dress, the type of language and the loose behavior at such affairs is completely alien and contrary to everything that Yiddishkeit stands for. It is clear, therefore, that if for business reasons one must attend such a party, he or she must do so only when there is no other choice, and even then, he or she must come and go as quickly as possible. Lingering in such an environment can lead to serious transgression of many Torah laws.

For further sources see here and there.

questions.title_en: When G-d spoke to a particular individual, does anybody else hear what He is saying?
questions.question: At one point, the whole world heard G-d during the revelation in Mt. Sinai, but when G-d specifically spoke to someone, could anyone have eavesdropped and heard what He said or could it be only heard by the person He was talking to? For example, if G-d was revealing a prophecy to a prophet and somehow, someone was in the vicinity where G-d and the prophet are communicating, could the bystander hear/be privy to what was being said/communicated?

answers.text:
In 1 Shmuel 3:1-10, G-d speaks to Samuel and Eli doesn't hear it:

1And the lad Samuel was serving the Lord before Eli. Now the word of the Lord was withheld in those days; vision had not broken through. 2And it was on that day, that Eli was lying in his place, and his eyes had begun to grow dim; he could not see. 3And the lamp of God had not yet gone out, and Samuel was lying down. In the Temple of the Lord, where the Ark of God was. 4The Lord called to Samuel, and he said, "Here I am." 5And he ran to Eli, and said, "Here I am, for you have called me." And he said, "I did not call. Go back and lie down." And he went and lay down. 6And the Lord continued to call again to Samuel, and Samuel arose, and went to Eli, and said, "Here I am, for you have called me.'' And he said, "I have not called, my son. Go back and lie down." 7Now, Samuel had not yet known the Lord, and the word of the Lord had not yet been revealed to him. 8And the Lord continued to call Samuel for the third time; and he arose and went to Eli, and said, "Here I am, for you called me." And Eli understood that that the Lord was calling the youth. 9And Eli said to Samuel, "Go, lie down. And it shall be, if He will call you, that you shall say, 'Speak, O Lord, for Your bondsman is listening.' " And Samuel went and lay down in his place. 10And the Lord came and stood, and He called as at the other times, "Samuel! Samuel!" And Samuel said, "Speak, for Your bondsman is listening."

The Alshich describes (Shir Hashirim 1:2) prophesy as Hashem speaking to someone through their soul. Even though "the ears hear", they are hearing internally.

The Sinai event was an exception, where Hashem tore open the heavens.

It seems the default case is that nobody else can hear, unless Hashem makes an exception.

questions.title_he: לחשוש למוות קרוב לגיל פטירת ההורים
questions.question:
שלום רב,
רש"י בפרשת תולדות, על דברי יצחק אבינו בפסוק: "לא ידעתי יום מותי", מביא את דברי רבי יהושע בן קרחה בבראשית רבה שאדם צריך לחשוש כשהוא מגיע ל-5 שנים קודם פטירת כל אחד מהוריו (ועד חמש שנים אחרי) והוא למד זאת מיצחק אבינו. אולם לפי רש"י יצחק היה בן 123, וזה רק 4 שנים פחות ממיתת שרה, שנפטרה בגיל 127. א7 כן, יש לשאול:
1. אם צריך לחשוש 5 שנים קודם, למה יצחק לא חשש בגיל 122 וחיכה עד 123?
2. אם יצחק חשש רק 4 שנים לפני גיל פטירת אימו, איך לומד מכאן רבי יהושע בן קרחה שיש לחשוש 5 שנים קודם?
3. הלכה למעשה (או הנהגה למעשה) כיצד ראוי לנהוג: לחשוש 4 שנים לפני או 5 שנים לפני? במה צריך להתבטא החשש הזה, מלבד לצוות על ביתו?

יתכן ומנין השנים לא מדויק והוא השתדל בסוף מאה עשרים ושתים שלפי חשבונו זה יצא 123, כדאי לחשוש חמש שנים לפני, ואז להשתדל לעשות לעשות מצוות חשובות מאד שלא הספיק קודם, כמו צדקה גדולה שתזכיר את שמו. (תרומת מבנה ספר תורה וכדומה) או לימוד לפי היכולת. (כל הרמב"ם, כל המדרשים, כל הזוהר, וכמובן כל התנ"ך לפי היכולת) כמובן גם לצוות את ביתו.

questions.title_he: הנחת תפילין של ראש אחרי השתלת שיער
questions.question:
שלום כבוד הרב 

אחרי השתלת שיער אסור להניח תפילין של ראש אלא רק של יד במשך 12 ימים.
ולא ניתן לתזמן את זה לפני חול המועד, כי הם לא עובדים לפי התנאים שלי.

יש אפשרות לוותר על תפילין של ראש לימים אלו ?
מאוד אשמח אם תגיד לי גם מה הטעם לתשובתך

מודה לך מראש
רוני

שלום וברכה
אומנם יש הגבלה רפואית להניח תפילין של ראש בהידוק הרצועות, אך אנשים שעשו את הניתוח אומרים שאפשר להניח את התפילין ממש בנחת, תוך כדי שאתה אוחז אותן בידך והן מונחות ממש ברפיון על הראש, ולא הזיק להם. 
יש למצוא את הדרך הנכונה שלא יעבור יום אחד ללא שתניח תפילין, במיוחד שזו פעולה אסתטית ולא רפואית, וכמובן שמצד שני לא להזיק לתוצאות ההשתלה.

בתפילת אחינו כל בית ישראל מבקשים על העומדים בין בים ובין ביבשה, האם מותר להוסיף לבקש על העומדים באוויר דהיינו במטוסים או אסור להוסיף ודי שיכוון לזה?

שלום וברכה
לא הייתי משנה את הנוסח.
א. כי שאין ידוע לנו על אנשים באוויר שהם במצוקה, ותפילה זו נועדה לאדם שהוא במצוקה עקבית וארוכה.
ב. כל שינוי כזה עלול להביא לבלבול ואולי אף למחלוקת.
אם תרצה להוסיף בצנעה, אין בכך איסור

questions.title_he: מצאתי גיפט קארד ללא סימנים מזהים
questions.question:
מצאתי באוטובס גיפט קארד על סך 500₪ שנראה חדש וחוץ ממספר הכרטיס אין עליו סימנים מזהים כמו שם או שם החברה..
מה עלי לעשות? 
להביא לנהג? לקחת לעצמי?

כפי שנכתב בתשובה הנ"ל
אדם שמוצא מעות שאין בהם סימן בדרך של נפילה - הרי הם שלו והוא יכול להשתמש בהם.

באופן פשוט כרטיס מתנה "גיפט כארד" שאין עליו סימן או שם וכל אדם שכרטיס זה נמצא ברשותו יכול להשתמש בו, נחשב לעניין זה כמעות הנמצאות בארנק.
כמובן - שאין חובת הכרזה.

אמנם, יש שטענו שבימינו אדם לא בודק את ארנקו ואת מלאי הכרטיסים שיש לו כל רגע וממילא יכול להיות שבזמן שמצאת את הכרטיס הוא עדין לא התייאש(ואין ביכולת המוצא לזכות בו).
אך רבים הפוסקים הסוברים שחז"ל קבעו זאת כדבר ברור ולא דנים באדם ספציפי או במציאות ספציפית אלא באופן כללי.

לדעות המחמירות נראה גם שמותר להשתמש אלא שאם יבא אדם ויטען שזה שלא ויגיד היכן נפל יש אומרים שנצטרך להחזיר לו.

אני לומדת קבלה של בעל סולם מותר או לא 
תודה

בעל הסולם היה אדם גדול ובודאי דברים קדושים. צריך ללמוד דברי קודש אלה בקדושה גדולה, צניעות, זהירות מלשון הרע, שמירת שבת כהלכה אמירת ברכות בכוונה ועוד. אם לא שומרים אז אין ללמוד דברי קודש גבוהים כל כך.

questions.title_en: Can you destroy property to save your life?
questions.question:
The Talmud [Bava Kamma 60b] discusses destroying property to save your life:

There were stacks of barley belonging to Jews in which the Philistines were hiding, and [King David wanted to burn down the stacks to kill the Philistines and save his own life]. He raised the dilemma: What is [the law?] [Is it permitted] to save oneself [by destroying] somebody else’s property?

questions.title_he: הוצאת ר' ירמיה מבית המדרש - אי אפשר לחנך בלי לפגוע?
questions.question:
כדי להראות לתלמידים האחרים שלא לתמוה על שיעורי רבנן צריך לפגוע בתלמיד ולהוציא אותו מבית המדרש?
למה לא לשאול את התלמיד מה היה מטרתו? ודאי שלא היה מטרתו לפגוע בשיעורי חז"ל אלא היה לו שאלה טובה.
אני פשוט לא מצליח להבין שזאת סיבה לפגוע בתלמיד.

שלום וברכה!

באופן כללי, קשה לדעת בוודאות מה בדיוק אירע באותו מעשה. כמו מעשים רבים אחרים שמופיעים בדברי חז"ל, גם המעשה הזה מסופר בקיצור ובתמצית, וייתכן מאד שהיו שם נקודות נוספות שאינן ידועות לנו והן משמעותיות כדי להבין את הסיטואציה לאשורה. 
אבל יש לשים לב לשתי נקודות:
ראשית, לא מדובר כאן בתלמיד צעיר. כאשר קוראים לאדם "רבי", ("רבי ירמיה"), משמעות הדבר היא שהוא סמוך, דהיינו שהוא כבר הוכר כתלמיד חכם ופוסק והתמנה כחבר בבית הדין (עיין סנהדרין י"ג ב; רש"י עבודה זרה ח' ב, ד"ה "דיני קנסות"). אם נשווה זאת למציאות בימינו – אם תלמיד בישיבה ישאל שאלה מוזרה נשתדל להתייחס אליו בסלחנות, אבל מר"מ בישיבה יש כמובן דרישות גבוהות יותר. יתרה מזו, אם ר"מ שואל בבית המדרש שאלות מוזרות, שיוצרות גיחוך אצל התלמידים, הדבר עלול לגרום לפגיעה בכבוד התורה ולגרום לזילות של לימוד התורה בעיני התלמידים.
בנוסף, כמה מפרשים מעירים (עיין בפירוש "כח שור" על הגמרא שם; תפארת ישראל, בועז, אבות ה', א) שבמקומות אחרים מתוארים מקרים דומים שבהם ר' ירמיה שואל שאלות על השיעורים שהגדירו חז"ל לעניינים הלכתיים שונים (עיין ראש השנה י"ג א; סוטה ט"ז ב). דהיינו שזו תופעה חוזרת ולא מקרה בודד. יתרה מזו, בפירוש "כח שור" מצביע על כך שבמקומות האחרים הזהירו את ר' זירא שלא ישאל שאלות מסוג זה, "לא תפיק נפשך לבר מהילכתא". מסתבר אם כן, שלאחר כמה פעמים שבהם ר' ירמיה שאל שאלות כאלה והוזהר, כאשר הוא שאל בכל זאת פעם נוספת שאלה מסוג זה החליטו להוציא אותו מבית המדרש.

בזמנינו אין נופלים אפים בפישוט ידים ורגליהם, והטעם העיקרי בזה משום שצריכים לזה ספר תורה ואין אנו בקיאים בחסירות ויתירות וחוששים שמא הוא פסול,  ויש לשאול שבירושלים שנוהגים שנופלים אפיים גם במקום שאין שם ספר תורה משום קדושת המקום, למה איננו נופלים בפישוט ידיים ורגלים כמנהג הגמרא?

הטעם שאמרת לא ידוע לנו. 
מקור נפ"א הוא מיהושע שנפל לפני הארון. ומכיון שאיננו רשאים להשוות את עצמנו ליהושע האשכנזים מסתפקים בהטיית הראש, וגם משום אבן משכית. והספרדים גם לא מטים את ראשם. 

בירושלים נוהגים ליפול על הפנים גם ללא ארון בגלל קדושתה, אך פישוט ידים ורגלים אסור גם בירושלים

questions.title_en: What do the literal meanings of "Af al pi" and "Af al gav" have to do with the actual meanings?
questions.question:
As far as I can tell, אף על פי/ Af Al Pi would literally translate to "nose on (my) mouth". Similarly, אף על גב/ Af Al Gav would literally translate to "nose on back". In actuality, they both mean "even though". Do mefarshim note this, and explain why this expression is worded the way it is?

From a quick sefaria search, it seems like the earliest source we have for either version is Tannaic - Mishna for Af Al Pi, Sifra for Af Al Gav.

questions.title_en: Esav's religious and Jewish status
questions.question: Is Esav still considered a Jew considering his parents being Yitzchak and Rivka, and having brit milah? Also, what was his religious status? Was he really an idol worshipper or just non-observant, perhaps even an atheist? Please cite sources, thanks.

answers.text:
The commentary Tosafos Daas Zekeinim on Bereshis 25:25 quotes a midrash without a reference, from which we can answer negatively about Eisav's circumcision:

ויצא הראשון אדמוני, “the first baby emerged, reddish looking;” according to a Midrash, when his father saw that, he concluded that the blood of the infant had not yet matured to the stage when he could be circumcised without that operation endangering his life, and that is why he delayed the date for the circumcision. Something similar is related in the Talmud, tractate Shabbat, folio 134, where Rabbi Nathan relates that he once met a lady who had lost two of her children as a result of circumcision. She asked him if she had to circumcise her third son also and risk losing him too. When Rabbi Nathan looked at the infant, he noted that his skin looked extremely red. He therefore told his mother to wait with circumcising him until this red skin would become normal looking. She did so, and circumcised him in due course and he survived without further problem. When Yitzchok waited a year or two for the skin colour of Esau to change and it did not happen, he assumed that this son was going to remain in that condition, but he still did not circumcise him. When he turned 13, he still restrained himself from circumcising him. He had waited all this time thinking that seeing he had not been circumcised at the age of eight days he would circumcise him at the age Yishmael had been circumcised. This is what was meant in the Book of Ezekiel chapter 35,6: אם לא דם שנאת ודם ירדפך, “surely though you have hated blood, blood shall pursue you.”

At the same time, the midrash Bereshis Rabba 76:9 states in affirmative that Eisav was circumcised:

“He arose during that night and he took his two wives, and his two maidservants, and his eleven children, and crossed the ford of the Yabok” (Genesis 32:23). “He arose during that night and he took his two wives, and his two maidservants…” – but where was Dina? He placed her in a chest and locked it with her in it. He said: ‘This wicked one has a covetous eye; [I do this] so he will not direct his eyes, see her, and take her from me.’ Rav Huna said in the name of Rabbi Abba HaKohen Bardela: The Holy One blessed be He said to him: ‘“For the sake of one who deprives his neighbor of kindness” (Job 6:14) – you withheld kindness from your neighbor, you withheld kindness from your brother. Had she married the man, she would not have engaged in licentiousness. You did not seek to marry her to a circumcised man, so she married an uncircumcised man. You did not seek to marry her in a permitted fashion, so she married in a prohibited fashion.’ That is what is written: “Dina daughter of Leah…went out” (Genesis 34:1).

This is resolved with the help of the commentary Yefeh Toar on Bereshis Rabba 76.9.3. The full published version by Machon Aharon states (unlike Sefaria):

We have a difficulty, above in p. 63:18 Eisav hates the blood of milla, i.e. consequently he was ערל (uncircumcized), and we cannot apply there principle that ערלי/uncircumcized of Israel are called מהולים/circumcized (as in mishna Nedarim 3:11), thus what we explained there - is fitting.

By Sefaria numbering, the reference is midrash Bereshis Rabba 63:13 (Sefaria uses different enumeration as compared to the edition of the midrash). The relevant words there:

Did Esau hate blood? Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥman said: This is the blood of birthright and offerings. Rabbi Levi said: זה דם מילה - This is the blood of circumcision. The Rabbis said: You hated a person’s blood in his body. That is what is written: “He loved curses, and they will now come upon him. [He had no desire for blessing, and it will now be far from him]” (Psalms 109:17).

Explans Yefeh Toar (in the Machon Aharon edition):

זה דם מילה: he pulled his orla, and all his children were uncircumcized.

As far as person's religious status, in Judaism either a person believes in G-d, or is a follower of Avodah Zara (foreign worship - anything but G-d). There is no distinction for atheism.

questions.title_en: How could Amram have seen Jacob given Biblical chronology?
questions.question: The Talmud says that Amram saw Jacob (Bava Batra 121b). But Exodus 12:40 says that the sons of Israel were in Egypt for 430 years. Aaron was 83 during the Exodus, and Amram lived to be 137, and Jacob lived to be 147. So this means that Jacob was born at most 367 years before the Exodus. So even if Ex 12:40 is talking about the time in Egypt and Canaan, how can this be possible because Israel himself didn't exist 430 years before the Exodus, so his sons couldn't have done anything. In fact not even Isaac existed 430 years before the Exodus.

answers.text: According to traditional Jewish sources, the sojourn in Egypt was 210 years. The number 430 refers to the length of time from the Covenant of the Pieces (ברית בין הבתרים) to the Exodus, which was defined as a kind of sojourn spread across Canaan, Goshen and Egypt. See e.g., Tanchuma Miketz 8:1; Rashi on Genesis 15:13; Rashi on Exodus 12:40 (based on Mechilta de-Rabbi Yishmael 14:15); Beresheet Rabbah 63:3; Seder Olam Rabbah ch. 3.

questions.title_en: Ha'azinu as a spiritual remedy for heretical thoughts
questions.question:
The B'nei Yissoschor in the sefer Agra D'Pirka, as quoted by the sefer Kavod Shabbos (Parshas Ha'azinu, p. 548) says:

לומר בכל יום שירת האזינו: נראה לי בסגולה ללמוד בכל יום שירת האזינו, והוא סגולה להנצל מאפיקורסות ומדעות הכוזביות

To recite the Song of Ha'azinu every day: It seems to me to be a worthwhile practice to study the Song of Haazinu every day, as it is a spiritual remedy (segulah) to be saved from heresy and false beliefs.

See also the Steipler Gaon in Kiryana D'Igarta (Vol. 1, letter 45):

I have also seen it brought in holy books that reciting the Song of Ha'azinu every day greatly dispels thoughts of heresy [though, of course, not immediately but over time]. Many years ago, someone came to me, lamenting about thoughts of heresy, heaven forbid. I told him what is mentioned in the holy books about reciting the Song of Ha'azinu, and he did so for several consecutive years. He later informed me that he was completely saved from these thoughts. May G-d help us for the sake of His Name.

What exactly is it about the Shir Ha'azinu that dispells heretical thoughts from a person? Are there any meforshim or sources that discuss this? Why especially Ha'azinu?

answers.text:
There is a fascinating article here which relates an amazing story about the Ramban and a student of his that became a heretic. Whilst the student starting by mocking his Rebbe, eventually they got talking about what made him reject yiddishkeit in its entirety. The student responded, “I heard from you that all the events from the creation of the world to the coming of the Moshiach, including the private things that will happen to every man of Israel, are all implied in the song of Haazinu. This seemed impossible to me and made me doubt everything I had learned from you.”

With this as an introduction, the article goes on to note that the Rebbe Rayetz also brings down the segula (refer to his Sefer Zichronos, cheilek alef, p. 125 4th par) and the article notes a tentative reason behind why Shiras Haazinu carries so much weight...

הרבי מליובאוויטש מבאר, כי שירת האזינו מהווה מכלול שלם של דרך חיים. החל מחסדי ה’ איתנו, דרך הפניית עורף מצידנו, התוצאה שנגרמת ממעשינו – ועד לגאולה העתידית. חלק התוכחה הם גם כן חלק מהשירה הכללית, ולא ניתן להתעלם, כאשר בוחנים את מסלול החיים המלא, מהקטעים הפחות נעימים. גם בהם, בגאולה העתידה, יתגלה כי הכל היה לטובה.

בסופו של דבר, השירה כולה מלמדת אותנו כי ‘הצור תמים פעלו’. גם כאשר ישנם מאורעות שאיננו מבינים, מדובר בתהליך שעלינו לעבור עד לגאולה העתידית, אז נגלה כי הכל היה לטובה. “א-ל אמונה ואין עול, צדיק וישר הוא”.

The Lubavitcher Rebbe explains that the Song of Haazinu constitutes a complete whole way of life. Starting from G-d's grace with us, through our turning away, the result of our actions – and up to the future redemption. The parts of the rebuke are also part of the general poem, and we cannot ignore, when examining the full course of life, the less pleasant parts. Even in them, in the future redemption, it will be revealed that everything was for the best.

Ultimately, the entire poem teaches us that ‘The Rock — whose deeds are perfect.’ Even when there are events that we do not understand, it is a process that we must go through until the future redemption, when we will discover that everything was for the best. “A faithful G-d, never false, true and upright indeed.”

So possibly one can suggest that since the whole song is rooted in the essence of life and alludes to G-d's all-powerful Omnipresence, that runs counter to any heretical thought.

Upon researching further, the Sefer Chikrei Minhagim (cheilek beis) brings down all the sources for the regular recitation of Haazinu, and notes a further idea that would perhaps answer this question (see over the page from the subtitle - "הפלאתה של פרשת האזינו" - "The wonder of Parshas Haazinu")

It notes that it is quoted in the name of the Ramban1 that:

כלולים כל המצוות וכל הדברים שבעולם

All the commandments and all the things in the world are included (in Parshas Haazinu).

In other words, Haazinu is significant. With a song that has such a deep rooted message, one that encompasses all the Mitzvos etc. arguably this is the strongest segula for heretical thoughts.

1 Note that this quote relates to the Ramban's interaction with his apostate student mentioned above. It is cited in several places including Seder HaDoros, cheilek alef, p.214 (left hand column, 7 lines up from the bottom) and also Kav HaYashar 23:5.

questions.title_en: Why is Judaism not universally relevant?
questions.question: Why are Noahide laws deemed sufficient for non-Jews while Jews are obligated to a distinct, more comprehensive system?

answers.text:
Sanhedrin 58b and 59a explain that gentiles who study the seven Mitzvot are considered like a kohen gadol, who undertakes the most holy service in the beit hamikdash. We have various traditions that a non-Jew can merit the World to Come for practicing these mitzvot and doing good deeds. While we are obligated to accept converts and treat them with kindness and the utmost respect, we do not attempt to convert anyone, with rare historical exceptions, such as in Yemen.

Makkot 23b shows Rabbi Simlai explaining that Jews have 613 mitzvot which we are obligated to learn and follow. This is why the seven mitzvot bnei Noach are not adequate for Jews.

questions.title_en: Can you daven in the same room as a sleeping person?
questions.question: If two Jewish people are in the same room, can one daven in that room if the other is asleep in the same room? Is there anything that would prohibit one from davening in the same room as a sleeping person?

answers.text:
If your issue is about reciting prayers when seeing something immodest, only if the sleeping person is not dressed properly and exposed can it be problematic (see SA OC Siman 74 and biur halacha there). But other than that, no issue should exist. This is clear by the fact that the poskim only discuss erva situations and similar issues and not the mere fact of someone sleeping.

There can be an issue of gezel sheina if you daven loud and wake the person up.

questions.title_en: Standards of a Place for Davening
questions.question:
Is a Jew allowed to daven in bed? Can one daven in their pajamas in a place? Can a Jew daven in the same room as an unmade bed?

PS: This question is alluding to ALL contexts (i.e. whether is person is sick, healthy, in a dorm, at home, etc.).

answers.text:
Dressing appropriately depends on the current trends and the setting, as well as how people behave in public and around important figures. If short sleeve shirts or sandals without socks are acceptable, there is usually no need to change for prayer. However, it is important to wear respectable clothing when standing before Hashem.

Piskei Teshuvot

There are significantly different halachos if a person is bedridden due to illness, c”v, as opposed to healthy. If a person is sick, CYLOR.

questions.title_en: Why do we intentionally not bless the festival after the haftarah on Shabbat Chol HaMoed Pesach?
questions.question:
On Shabbat Chol haMoed Pesach, all of my Ashkenaz siddurim will tell you to make the regular Shabbat blessing as the final one after the reading of the Haftarah. This is different than the instruction on Shabbat Chol haMoed Sukkot, where one makes a blessing that also includes the festival.

One might initially think this is the same principle or pattern applied as Why is Hallel different in Sukkot and Pesach (chol ha-moed)? i.e. the ongoing use of lulav and unique sacrifices make Sukkot a special day each day. The Torah service would be consistent in that sense with the Hallel that came before except . . .

Relatively soon afterwards on that same morning, you are going to make that same blessing: מְקַדֵּשׁ הַשַּׁבָּת וְיִשרָאֵל וְהַזְמַנִּים as you do throughout the festival during Musaf. It is perfectly appropriate thing to say there, but highlights the question: why would that be inappropriate during the Torah service? It makes the explicit choice to only mention Shabbat after the Haftarah look more like an intentional exception.

What is the reason that our tradition is to explicitly not mention the festival at this point?

It also strikes me that this is in some sense different stakes than the question about Hallel. Making a berakah or which one to make is a different, possibly weightier, thing than saying more or fewer Psalms. Is this a misconception?

questions.question: In relation to this question that I have asked. What is the correct English translation or equivalent of the Hebrew word מין?

questions.title_en: Source for Hiddush on Parashat Bereshit
questions.question:
It says in Parashat Bereshit:

וַיְבָ֣רֶךְ אֹתָם֮ אֱלֹהִים֒ וַיֹּ֨אמֶר לָהֶ֜ם אֱלֹהִ֗ים פְּר֥וּ וּרְב֛וּ וּמִלְא֥וּ אֶת־הָאָ֖רֶץ וְכִבְשֻׁ֑הָ וּרְד֞וּ בִּדְגַ֤ת הַיָּם֙ וּבְע֣וֹף הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם וּבְכׇל־חַיָּ֖ה הָֽרֹמֶ֥שֶׂת עַל־הָאָֽרֶץ׃ God blessed them and God said to them, “Be fertile and increase

It is generally understood that the first words Hashem spoke to humanity are פרו ורבו , but this Shabbat I realized that the second Elohim is superfluous and had a Hiddush concerning this verse:

The first thing Hashem says to humanity is "Elohim" like it says in Psalms "Elohim Atem!" Meaning: You have the power to rule! And only then comes the Mitzva of Pru uRvu.

So the verse can be read as :

!"וַיְבָ֣רֶךְ אֹתָם֮ אֱלֹהִים֒ וַיֹּ֨אמֶר לָהֶ֜ם: "אֱלֹהִ֗ים

I am sure I am not the first one to have this idea. Can anyone tell me which commentary already said this?

questions.title_en: Isru Chag on Shabbos
questions.question:
Sukkah 45b:

״אִסְרוּ חַג בַּעֲבוֹתִים עַד קַרְנוֹת הַמִּזְבֵּחַ״. אָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי, וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן הַמָּחוֹזִי מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן הַמָּכוֹתִי: כׇּל הָעוֹשֶׂה אִיסּוּר לֶחָג בַּאֲכִילָה וּשְׁתִיָּה, מַעֲלֶה עָלָיו הַכָּתוּב כְּאִילּוּ בָּנָה מִזְבֵּחַ וְהִקְרִיב עָלָיו קׇרְבָּן, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״אִסְרוּ חַג בַּעֲבוֹתִים עַד קַרְנוֹת הַמִּזְבֵּחַ״.

Bind [isru] with dense-leaved branches [ba’avotim] on the Festival until the horns of the altar” (Psalms 118:27), which alludes to both the binding of the lulav and to the myrtle branch, referred to in the Torah as the branch of a dense-leaved tree [anaf etz avot]. Rabbi Yirmeya said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai, and Rabbi Yoḥanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon HaMeḥozi, who said in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan HaMakkoti: With regard to anyone who establishes an addition [issur] to the Festival on the day after the Festival by eating and drinking, the verse ascribes him credit as though he built an altar and sacrificed an offering upon it, as it is stated: “Add [isru] to the Festival with fattened animals [ba’avotim] until the horns of the altar.”

If the day following Yom Tov is Shabbos (as it was this year in the diaspora), is there any reason to increase in eating and drinking on Sunday (since doing so on Shabbos, which is already festive, might not demonstrate an “Issur Lachag”)?

questions.title_en: During the Mabul, did birds die first or last?
questions.question:
Bereishis 7:21 implies the birds died first in the Mabul:

וַיִּגְוַע כָּל־בָּשָׂר הָרֹמֵשׂ עַל־הָאָרֶץ בָּעוֹף וּבַבְּהֵמָה וּבַחַיָּה וּבְכָל־הַשֶּׁרֶץ הַשֹּׁרֵץ עַל־הָאָרֶץ וְכֹל הָאָדָם׃ - And all flesh that stirred on earth perished — birds, cattle, beasts, and all the things that swarmed upon the earth, and all humankind.

However, two pesukim later (7:23) implies the birds died last:

וַיִּמַח אֶת־כָּל־הַיְקוּם אֲשֶׁר עַל־פְּנֵי הָאֲדָמָה מֵאָדָם עַד־בְּהֵמָה עַד־רֶמֶשׂ וְעַד־עוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם וַיִּמָּחוּ מִן־הָאָרֶץ וַיִשָּׁאֶר אַךְ־נֹחַ וַאֲשֶׁר אִתּוֹ בַּתֵּבָה׃ - All existence on earth was blotted out—humans, cattle, creeping things, and birds of the sky; they were blotted out from the earth. Only Noah was left, and those with him in the ark.

Although maybe the birds were struck first by the heavy rainfall, they also could have flown to the highest available points then hovered for longer - when did they die in the flood?

answers.text:
Ostriches died first because they stupidly buried their heads in the flooded dirt.

Job 39:17 For God caused her to forget wisdom, and He did not give her a share of understanding.

The rest of the birds died last because they could fly to the tops of mountains.

Thank you for the humor Clint Eastwood. The obvious answer is that all creatures died at about the same time. The two orders of verses are a testament to this fact. In a number of other cases the Torah reverses the order to show that there is not special preference to either term mentioned. The most famous is Shemos 20:12 and Devarim 5:16 mitzvah of honoring parents with father preceding the mother:

Honor your father and your mother, that you may long endure on the land that your God Hashem is assigning to you.

Honor your father and your mother, as your G-d Hashem has commanded you, that you may long endure, and that you may fare well, in the land that your G-d Hashem is assigning to you.

When describing the mitzvah of reverence the order is reversed Vayikra 19:3:

You shall each revere your mother and your father, and keep My sabbaths: I Hashem am your God.

The obvious halakhic consequence: "The laws of honor and reverence are equally relevant with regard to one's father and mother" (Rabbi Moshe Lieber "The Fifth Commandment" Chapter 1, section A halacha 2).

questions.title_he: אם הכל הבל הבלים, אז למה לי ללכת בדרכי התורה, הדת והאמונה?
questions.question:
שלמה המלך אמר שהכל בחיים הבל הבלים, הכל בעצם חסר משמעות, אז למה אנחנו צריכים את התורה בכלל? ברור שאנחנו נותנים בעצם משמעות לכל דבר בחיינו, וגם ברור שאפשר להסתכל על זה גם בצורה חיובית וגם בצורה שלילית, אבל אני שואלת שאלה אחרת… למה לא לעשות פשוט מה שבא לי מבלי לחשבן? הרי הכל חסר משמעות? למה לא לחטוא בעצם? הרי הכל הבל הבלים… 

שלום
שלמה המלך הספר קוהלת בא לומר לאדם: שענייני העולם הזה(!) הם הבל הבלים, דבר שאין בו ממש. אין הם מטרה כשלעצמם, לא ניתן לראות בעולם הזה את תכלית הכל.
אך ברור לשלמה כפי שהוא מסיים את ספר קהלת "סוֹף דָּבָר הַכֹּל נִשְׁמָע אֶת האלוקים יְרָא וְאֶת מִצְו‍ֹתָיו שְׁמוֹר כִּי זֶה כָּל הָאָדָם" וכפי שכתב רש"י: "כי לדבר הזה נברא כל האדם". יש תועלת ומטרה בעולם הזה, יש תכלית לחיינו, וכאשר נממש אותה נחייה מתוך משמעות וקדושה תועלת וחיות.
בהצלחה רבה

questions.title_en: Can We Use Our Reward In The Next World Like Money In This World?
questions.question:
A story about the Vilna Ga’on appears in Halachic Man (on p.30 in the 1984 English edition). I feel like I’ve heard essentially the same story many times, told about various historical figures, although I cannot now remember. In Halachic Man, the author refers to the story as a folk legend.

In the story, the Vilna Ga’on is unable to obtain Hadassim that he needs to perform one of the commandments of Sukkot. He sends people out to search, and Hadassim are found, growing in a particular woman’s yard. She agrees to sell them to the Vilna Ga’on, but the price that she demands is the reward that the Vilna Ga’on should receive for performing the Mitzvah. He agrees to the price and is, surprisingly, very happy when performing the Mitzvah on these terms. He explains that he is now able to perform the Mitzvah not for the sake of receiving a reward.

I have several problems with this story.

  1. In the internal logic, it seems strange that Hadassim are growing in this woman’s yard but no place else. The climate and soil permit cultivation, and need for Hadassim on Sukkot should have taken nobody by surprise.
  2. Also in the internal logic, there seems to be no reason for the Vilna Ga’on to have been happy on this particular occasion, if he could have made the same arrangement on every occasion. Similarly, if any of you would like to assign to me all of the reward for your performance of Mitzvos, you need only say the word.
  3. Stepping outside of the internal logic now, how could our reward in the next world be like money that we can spend in this world? Could we set up an economy on this basis, paying for groceries and babysitting with a share of our reward in the next life? Could a rich man go around to all of the poor people, buying their reward on the cheap, depending only on their misfortune in needing money? This way of thinking about reward is repellant in that it undermines the justice of reward and punishment, which is seemingly the whole point of reward and punishment.
  4. The Vilna Ga’on died in 1797. The original Hebrew text of Halachic man was published in 1944. The English edition that I saw provides no source for the story.
  5. I cannot think of any old telling of any comparable story. For example, in the story (Avodah Zarah 18) about the execution of Chanania Ben Tradyon, someone sacrifices his own life to help, after assurance that he will receive a share in the world to come, and the story then assures us that he did receive that reward. And in the relationship between Zevulun and Issachar that Rashi mentions (Gen 49:13, Deut 33:18), Zevulun works to support Issachar in learning; and everyone I ask seems to understand some sort of implication for the reward each party receives. But in these stories, everyone is genuinely doing something meritorious, and the reward could simply by commensurate with the desert. That seems clearly not the intention in the story of the Vilna Ga’on. In the Vilna Ga’on story, the idea seems to be that the woman is receiving more reward than her actions really recommend, simply because she drove a hard bargain; and her reward is at the expense of the party actually deserving of the reward, so that nobody seems to be getting reward according to his merit.

So, I ask you.

Can you point me to authoritative sources for this idea that while we live, we can use our future reward as money for the payment of our bills, so that in the end these arrangements will actually transfer reward from the otherwise deserving party to the otherwise undeserving party? Is there any way to improve the provenance of this Vilna Ga’on story, or comparable “Gedolim” stories? Are there relevant ancient, medieval or Renaissance versions?

answers.text:
The premise behind your question is logically compelling. How can 'future reward' be transferred from one to another like a form of currency? And, indeed, there are numerous sources - most notably, R' Hai Gaon [quoted by Maharam Alashkar (Siman 101) and cited by R' Akiva Eger (Hil. Talmud Torah)], who decry the concept of buying or selling reward.

Your question asks for authoritative sources for such a concept. If you accept the Vilna Gaon as authoritative, you probably will be happy with a source from his disciple R' Chaim Volozhin. In Ruach Chaim (commentary to Avos, 1:1) R' Chaim Volozhin tells the story of the author of Turei Zahav (known as the 'Taz'), who 'donated' the reward of one study session to a sick child, who recovered in that merit.

A century before the Taz (1586-1667), Shiltei Giborim (d. 1557) in his glosses to Rif (Baba Kama 32b) indicates this idea - that one can effectively sell his divine reward for money - although he provides a caveat that the sale takes place prior to performing the mitzvah. [See, however, Shu"t Meishiv Davar 14 for a different understanding].

ולפ"ז יעלה יפה מה שכתבתי דאדם יכול למכור המצות שלו ויעלו לאיש הקונה דהא יש להם ערך י' זהובים לאחר מיהו נראה דוקא מועיל הקנין במצוה שעתיד לעשות אבל לא במצוה שעשה כבר

Imrei Binah (Responsa, Siman 13) attempts to reconcile the opinions by differentiating between two types of 'divine reward'. See also this answer

questions.title_en: How did the Briskers, or the Soloveitchiks, acquire the reputation for exactingness in quotation?
questions.question:
I recently came across a story about the Vilna Ga’on in Halachic Man (on p.30 in the 1984 English edition). I had various doubts about the authenticity of the story, and in the course of discussing my doubts with several people I kept hearing the assurance that the Briskers, or the Soloveitchiks, are very careful about such things and can be trusted to tell the story only because they have authenticated it.

How did the Briskers or the Soloveitchiks acquire this reputation for this sort of exactingness?

answers.text: They probably obtained their reputation for precision because their Method emphasizes precisely defining concepts beforehand to better to understand difficulties in Gemara. They probably underwent flanderization and gained a reputation as sticklers and fact checkers overall.

questions.title_en: The famous Morid HaGeshem vs. Goshem debate as it relates to Morid HaTal
questions.question:
Just to establish some basic grammar rules quickly - if a word starts with two segols and is the end of a sentence, the first segol is often changed to a kamatz (one example of many in the Torah: Yefes turns into Yufes when the note is an esnachta or it's a sof passuk). Similarly, a patach will be changed to a kamatz if it's the end of a sentence (maaluh --> muluh).

There's a famous debate among poskim quoted in several answers to this question about whether the line of Mashiv HaRuach ends in Morid HaGeshem or Morid HaGushem, a segol under the gimmel or a kamatz. However it seems to be more or less universal among those who say Morid HaTal to say it with a kamatz under the tess (Morid HaT-uh-l instead of Morid HaT-ah-l). Rav Shlomo Zalman Aurbach is quoted in a Dirshu Mishna Brurah note in Siman 114 as saying it should be a patach but every siddur I've seen has it as a kamatz. Assuming there's basis for pronouncing Tul with a kamatz, which indicates that whatever line you're saying before Mechalkel is separate and has a stoppage before Mechalkel, why would you say Morid HaGeshem with a segol, which implies the line continues into Mechalkel? As it happens, R' SZ Aurbach is quoted in that same Dirshu note as saying it should be Geshem with a segol, so the question would not be on him, but most siddurim have the pronunciation of Geshem with a segol and Tul with a Kamatz.

answers.text:
This answer is from Emes L'Yaakov Al HaTorah, p. מ״ו-מ״ז.

First of all, it seems the custom of the Stoliner Chasidim is indeed to say "tal" with a patach, as you would have expected.

But the reason to differentiate between "geshem" and "tul" is that "tul" goes with the previous phrase and ends it, because "tul" is involved in the mechanism of techiyas hameisim (cf. Isaiah 26:19), whereas "geshem" is at the beginning of a list of other gevuros of Hashem.

In Mishnaic Hebrew, segolates completely lack a pausal form. Their vowels remain the same regardless of their position in a sentence. When the phrase משיב הרוח ומוריד הגשם was first instituted, the final word was pronounced הַגֶּשֶׁם, without a Kamatz.

There’s a wider debate regarding whether blessings and parts of the liturgy that were authored using Mishnaic Hebrew, should be pronounced as if they were written using Biblical Hebrew. That debate is the same reason that, in the blessing over wine, most Ashkenazim say הַגָּפֶן with a Kamatz, while Sephardim pronounce it with two Segols.

The reason most Ashkenazim pronounce הגשׁם with a Kamatz, is because it probably does come at the end of a sentence; thus, if it were Biblical Hebrew, we would all pronounce it with a Kamatz. However, as mentioned, the word’s position didn’t matter in Mishnaic Hebrew.

This debate does not apply to the word הַטָּל. In the summer months, the entire phrase of משיב הרוח is replaced by מוריד הטל. If the word “הגשׁם” is at the end of a sentence, so is הטל. A stressed Patach vowel, unlike segolates, does have a pausal form in Mishnaic Hebrew, in which the Patach lengthened to a Kamatz.

Thus, according to the majority opinion that this phrase occurs at the end of a sentence, the word הטל would have a Kamatz. According to the minority opinion that it instead begins the next sentence, it would have a Patach.

questions.title_he: הגדרת לשון הרע רכילות והוצאת שם רע
questions.question:
מה ההבדל בין לשון הרע לרכילות?

ישנם שלושה מושגים, לשון הרע, הוצאת שם רע ורכילות. ונבאר את שלושתם. 

לשון הרע: כשאדם מספר על חבירו דברים אמיתיים אך רעים. כגון לספר על פלוני שהוא גנב.

הוצאת שם רע: אדם מספר על חבירו דברים רעים וגם שקריים.

רכילות: מספר על חבירו דבר שאינו שלילי מצד עצמו, אך יכול לגרום למתח ולפגיעה באהבה בינהם. למשל, ראובן חגג בר מצווה לבנו, למחרת סיפר שמעון לראובן שגדי עזב את החגיגה בשעה מוקדמת, ידיעה זו אין בה גנאי מצד עצמה, אך מהווה רכילות, מאחר ויכולה להרחיק בין ראובן לגדי.

questions.title_en: Does one need to repeat Birchas Hamazon if he forgot Ya’aleh Veyavo after washing again for the Afikoman?
questions.question: If one forgot to eat the Afikoman, and he remembered after he bentched, so he washed again and ate the Afikoman, and then bentched again, and he forgot Ya’aleh Veyavo in the second bentching, must he repeat Birchas Hamazon?

answers.text:
M”B 188:26

מפני שאינו חייב וכו' - דדוקא בשבת וביו"ט שמחויב לאכול דוקא פת וא"כ חיוב ברהמ"ז קבוע הוא בימים האלה לכן תקינו רבנן לעיכובא ג"כ להזכיר שם מעין המאורע וכמו בתפלה … וכתב המ"א דה"ה ביו"ט יותר מסעודה אחת ביום וסעודה אחת בלילה שמחויב לאכול אם אכל ושכח להזכיר מעין המאורע בבהמ"ז אינו צריך לחזור כמו בר"ח אם לא כשלא אכל הסעודה בלילה שמחויב לאכול ביום שתים כדלקמן בסימן תקצ"ט דאז אפילו בסעודה שניה חוזר [פמ"ג]

One who forgot Yaaleh V’yavo must repeat Birkas Hamazon only after a seudah in which he was obligated to eat bread. In this case, although one who forgot Afikoman must wash again, the obligation is not certain, as per Shulchan Aruch O”C 477:2:

אם שכח ולא אכל אפיקומן ולא נזכר… עד אחר שבירך בורא פרי הגפן לא יאכל האפיקומן ויסמוך על מצה שאכל בתוך הסעוד' שכולן שמורות הן משעת לישה. אבל במקום שנהגו לעשו' שימור למצת מצוה משע' קצירה אפילו לא זכר עד אחר ההלל יטול ידיו ויברך המוציא ויאכל האפיקומן:

If one already made a brachah on the wine before remembering the Afikoman, one need not wash again and instead relies on the Matzah he already ate.

Clearly, the obligation to re-wash is a safek, in which case we do not repeat Birkas Hamazon. (Since the biblical obligation of Birkas Hamazon was already fulfilled. However, in general if one is unsure whether he said Yaaleh V’yavo it is not considered a safek, as it is assumed that he did not.)

The question would, however, remain in the latter case of the S”A quoted, which rules that one has until now only eaten Matzah that is shemurah mishaas ketzirah must wash again.

Here, one is certainly obligated to eat bread. The question, then, would be: is this special status given to any seudah one is personally obligated to eat, or is it limited to the amount of seudos the day requires one to eat?

[The M”B quoted above seems to suggest the latter understanding (“…since the chiyuv of Birkas Hamazon is fixed in these days…”), while the Magen Avraham he quotes points to a more individual chiyuv. See Shaarei Teshuvah 291:1 and the Machzik Brachah that he references, who opines that a seudah must be both required and usual in order to warrant re-bentching.]

questions.title_he: לבוש צנוע – אורך החצאית והשרוול, לעומת המקובל בחברה
questions.question:
בהמשך לשאלה שהיה כתוב בה שיש אפשרות חצאית עד הברך, אני מאוד רוצה להחמיר ולשים חצאית, אך רוב הסביבה שלי הולכות עם חצאיות קצרות יחסית וחולצות קצרות גם כן, מדי פעם ארוכות אבל לרוב קצר. ואני רוצה להשתדל בלי נדר לנסות לשים לב שזה לא יהיה קצר ממש כזה, לשים עד הברך. ברוך ה' אני משתדלת לשים חולצה עד המרפק לפחות וחצאית משתדלת בלי נדר שתגיע עד הברך, אך לא ידעתי שראוי להחמיר ולשים עד סוף הרגל, ואני מאוד רוצה כי חשוב לי להקפיד בהרבה דברים ולא בא לי "ליפול" בזה. זה חשוב לי, ומצד שני רוב הסביבה, בנות מהכיתה שלי, עם חצאיות קצרות/עד הברך. כן יש לפעמים ארוכות, אבל זה גם וגם כזה, אז זה טוב שאני אשים עד הברך? ואם כן אני חייבת לשים מתחת גרביון? אני באולפנה תורנית ואין כל כך בנות כאלה ששמות גרביון  מתחת לחצאיות ואני רוצה להרגיש בנוח... אבל אני גם מאוד רוצה ללכת בדרך הנכונה, רק שאני לא כל כך יודעת מה לעשות.
וגם בקשר לחולצות, באולפנה שלי בדרך כלל בקיץ רוב הבנות בכיתה שמות חולצות קצרות/עד המרפק בעיקר עד המרפק.. /    3/4 וראיתי שראוי לשים חולצה ארוכה, וזה פוגש אותי לדוגמה שנפגשים בסניף, ורובם עם חולצות קצרות וחצאיות קצרות, ואני כזה רוצה להשתדל לשים עד המרפק וחצאית שמכסה את הברך, אבל אם אני אשים חולצה ארוכה אני מרגישה שאהיה שונה מן השאר.. ועוד פעם זה חוזר על זה שבא לי באמת להתחזק בזה ולהתלבש צנוע אבל זה מאוד קשה שרוב הסביבה שלי בתנועת הנוער/ובכיתה לא מלבשים ככה
האם זה טוב לשים חולצה 3/4 /עד המרפק וחצאית עד הברך [ללא גרביון/טייץ]..?אני באמת רוצה תשובה גם אם אני אצטרך כבר לא להשתמש בבגדים שיש לי או להיות שונה מהשאר חשוב לי להקפיד אני מאוד מאמינה בלי עין הרע ברוך ה 
ואני רוצה להיות כמה שיותר בהשתדלות בלי נדר לנסות יותר טוב
אשמח לתשובה..
תודה רבה מראש

שלום וברכה!

כפי שהוסבר בתשובה הקודמת, לגבי כיסוי החלק של הרגל שמתחת לברך ישנן דעות שונות (פירוט נוסף מופיע בתשובה כאן: https://www.yeshiva.org.il/ask/123145). למעשה, מעיקר הדין יש מקום לסמוך על הדעה המקילה, דהיינו שיש להקפיד לכסות עד הברך ואת הברך עצמה אבל אין חובה לכסות גם את החלק התחתון של הרגל. על פי זה יוצא שמי שלובשת חצאית שמכסה את הברך אינה חייבת ללבוש גם גרביון – יש בכך מעלה, אבל זו לא חובה.
לגבי השרוולים – מוסכם בפוסקים שמן הדין השרוול צריך לכסות עד המרפק, ואין חובה לכסות את החלק שבין המרפק לבין כף היד.
לכן אם בסביבה שלך לא מקובל ללבוש חצאיות ארוכות, את יכולה להסתפק בחצאית שמכסה את הברך, ואת לא חייבת ללבוש גם גרביון בנוסף לחצאית. לפעמים אין ברירה אלא להיות שונה משאר החברה - למשל אם בסביבה שלך מקובל ללבוש חצאיות קצרות או שרוולים קצרים, אז באמת אין ברירה אלא להיות שונה וללבוש חצאית שמכסה את הברך ושרוולים עד המרפק, כיוון שלבוש כזה הוא חובה מעיקר הדין. אבל כאשר את מקיימת את ההלכה על פי עיקר הדין, את לא צריכה להתאמץ יותר וללבוש חצאית ארוכה עד הקרסול או גרביון, כאשר זה לא מקובל בסביבה שלך ויגרום לך להרגיש חריגה.

questions.title_he: האם מותר לכתוב ספר בהשראה מסיפור מהתנ"ך אבל עם שינויים?
questions.question:
שלום, אני מאוד אוהבת לכתוב סיפורי חול, ורציתי לדעת אם אני יכולה לקחת סיפור מהתנ"ך ולתת לסיפור תוספות וקצת פנטזיה לספר שלי, או שאסור לשנות סיפור מהתורה? 
תודה מראש :)

לשואלת, שלום וברכה!

סיפורי התורה נועדו להעביר לנו מסרים מסוימים. אם מוסיפים לסיפור תוספות, צריך לחשוב האם התוספת תורמת להעברת המסר, או חלילה להיפך. האם את רותמת את עצמך לשירותו של המסר, או שמא את "משתמשת" בדמויות המקראיות ובסיפור לצרכייך ולוקחת אותם לכיוון אחר.  

כדי להצליח במשימה הזו לא מספיק רצון טוב. כל סיפור שתחברי הוא בעצם כמו פירוש לתורה: מה היו הנסיבות ברקע (מדיני, חברתי, כלכלי, ועוד), מה היו המניעים של "גיבור הסיפור", מה התוצאות ממעשיו, וכדומה. זה דורש הרבה מאוד לימוד תורה ולימוד היסטוריה, הקשבה אמיתית בענווה אל מה שמקופל במילות התורה המעטות, לדמיין את הסיטואציה בכל רוחבה ועומקה ואת המתחולל בנפשות כל המעורבים, ואז לגשת ולכתוב את הסיפור (דוגמה חיובית לטעמי: ספריה של הסופרת אורנה בורדמן, שחלק מהם קראתי).

בהצלחה!

questions.title_en: Evening Too is a Time to Perform Mitzvot; How, Without Tzizit, do we Effectively Remember/Trigger Their Performance?
questions.question:
Premise #1: Mitzvot are performed by day and night. This idea really needs no proof, but I cite a Kesef Mishna (Laws of Shema 1:2) nonetheless: "לפי שמעשה המצות שנזכר בוהיה אם שמוע נוהג בין ביום בין בלילה" - "the performance of Mitzvot that is mentioned in the second paragraph of Shema occurs by day and night..."

Premise #2: Tzizit's purpose is to remind us to perform the mitzvot; the Tzizit-reminder only occurs by day. The same Kesef Mishna: וזכירת המצות שעל ידי ציצית שנזכר בויאמר אינו נוהג אלא ביום" - the Mitzvot reminder via Tzizit that is mentioned in the third paragraph of Shema only operates during the day"

Premise #3: the reason that the reminder mechanism of Tzizit can only be utilized by day is because one can only see Tzizit via daylight (and not in the dark). Duh!

Premise #4: ONLY the seeing of Tzizit (wearing a rubber band on your wrist or uttering verses of the Torah or utilizing sticky notes are NOT fully effective Mitzvot reminders) triggers an effective Mitzvot-reminder that, in turn, leads to the performance of Mitzvot: (Menachot 43b and Lechem Mishna cited below).

ותניא אידך וראיתם אותו וזכרתם ועשיתם ראיה מביאה לידי זכירה זכירה מביאה לידי עשיה And it is taught in another baraita: The verse states: “That you may look upon IT and remember all the commandments of the Lord and do them.” This teaches that looking at the ritual fringes leads to remembering the mitzvot, and remembering them leads to doing them.

The Lechem Mishna sums up this Premise #4 well: כיון שאין הזכירה באה אלא ע״י ציצית כמש״ה וראיתם אותו וזכרתם “Since the remembering ONLY comes via tzizit as it states ‘you shall see them and remember …’”

Question - evening too is a time to perform Mitzvot; how, without Tzizit, do we remember and thus trigger an evening performance? Put it another way - why did God create a daytime-only reminder for Mitzvot that occur day and night?

A possible answer - a dose of a daytime, visual Tzizit Mitzvot-reminder is sufficient to last through the evening too. Thoughts?

Unfortunately, several of the comments below fail to account for the Gemarra and Lechem Mishna cited here which support Premise #4 - Lechem Mishna (Gimmel):

answers.text:
Since you're asking for thoughts and not sources:

During the day you can see your Tzizit, but you also see everything else, hence you are constantly being distracted. Tzizit are there to help you refocus.

During the night you cannot see anything, and thus can concentrate on the task at hand. No need for Tzizit to refocus. Keeping in mind that when you can't see anything, you can't do much; you either sleep or use candlelight for specific tasks.

A final thought: Chazal teach us (Eruvin 65a) that the night was created for learning Torah, and while learning there is no need for constant reminders to do Mitzvot.

One can use the same idea as expressed in Gemara Menachos 43b in a slightly different context.

The Sages taught in a baraita: The Jewish people are beloved, as the Holy One, Blessed be He, surrounded them with mitzvot: They have tefilin on their heads, and tefilin on their arms, and tzitzis on their garments, and a mezuza for their doorways. Concerning them David said: “Seven times a day I praise You, because of Your righteous ordinances” (Psalms 119:164). This alludes to the two tefilin, the four tzitziot, and the mezuza, which total seven.

And when David entered the bathhouse and saw himself standing naked, he said: Woe to me that that I stand naked without any mitzva. But once he remembered the mitzva of circumcision that was in his flesh his mind was put at ease, as he realized he was still accompanied by this mitzva. After he left the bathhouse, he recited a song about the mitzva of circumcision, as it is stated in the verse: “For the leader, on the Sheminith: A Psalm of David” (Psalms 12:1). This is interpreted as a psalm about circumcision, which was given to be performed on the eighth [bashemini] day of the baby’s life.

The point here that we actually have 8 markers to remind us about all the mitzvos. Tefilin and mezuzah contain parshios, such as 2 paragraphs of Shema', that have requirement of performance of mitzvos by day and by night just like the tzitzis by day. We still have mezuzos on doorposts of our houses at night. Also bris-millah is a reminder by virtue of gematria ברי"ת = 612, i.e. it is itself a mitzvah and reminds us about other 612.
